stem: A 67-year-old man comes to the office with a 6-month history of decreased vision in his right eye; there is no pain.  Medical history is significant for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with periodic exacerbations.  He takes a muscarinic antagonist, as well as multivitamins, and uses corticosteroid inhalers.  He drinks 3 or 4 alcoholic beverages per week and has smoked a pack of cigarettes per day for the past 45 years.  Vital signs are normal.  BMI is 28 kg/m2.  Funduscopic examination of the right eye shows several bright, yellow, refractile deposits scattered around the central retina; the left fundus appears normal.  Which of the following is the greatest risk factor for development of this patient's condition?​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​​​​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌​​​​​​​​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​​‌​​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​​​‌​​​‌‌​​‌​​‌​​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌​​​​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌
explanation:
This patient with painless vision loss and yellow deposits (ie, drusen) around the central retina likely has age-related macular degeneration (AMD).  Aside from aging, tobacco use is the greatest risk factor because both conditions increase oxidative stress, which is central to AMD pathogenesis.

Oxidative damage causes dysfunction of the retinal pigmented epithelium (RPE), which contains the glial support cells for photoreceptors.  These glial cells normally secrete nutrients and metabolize waste products.  RPE dysfunction results in microglia activation (inflammation) and accumulation of waste products (ie, drusen).  This leads to death of the overlying photoreceptors.

The photoreceptors around the macula are more susceptible because of the increased metabolic requirements of high-resolution central vision.  This results in gradual central vision loss that often impacts driving, reading, and recognition of faces.  Smoking cessation should be emphasized in all patients to help reduce disease progression.

(Choice A)  Although heavy alcohol use may worsen AMD, the association is much weaker than with smoking.  Furthermore, mild to moderate alcohol consumption (like in this patient) may reduce AMD progression.

(Choice B)  Corticosteroids increase the risk for several age-related eye disorders (eg, glaucoma, cataracts) but not AMD.

(Choice C)  Antioxidants (eg, vitamins C and E, zinc, copper, lutein, zeaxanthin) can help slow AMD progression.  Vitamin excess is not associated with increased risk of AMD.

(Choice D)  Inhaled muscarinic antagonists (like other anticholinergic therapies) can cause vision loss by inducing acute angle-closure glaucoma.  This condition typically presents with eye pain, corneal edema, conjunctival redness, and a middilated pupil.

Educational objective:Age-related macular degeneration presents with painless central vision loss.  It results from oxidative damage to the retinal pigment epithelium, which induces inflammation (microglia activation) and waste product accumulation (drusen formation) that culminates in photoreceptor death.  Aside from aging, the greatest risk factor is tobacco use.​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​​​​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌​​​​​​​​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​​‌​​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​​​‌​​​‌‌​​‌​​‌​​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌​​​​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌
